quests.faultySentence: Me and my brother are going to the concert tonight.
quests.correctedSentence: My brother and I are going to the concert tonight.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since this pronoun is the subject performing the action, it needs the subject form 'I'; it's also more natural to place 'my brother and I' rather than starting with 'me'.
quests.nativeTip: As the subject of the sentence, should you use 'me' or 'I'?

quests.conceptTitle: Pronoun Case: Object Pronouns After Prepositions
quests.faultySentence: The manager gave the assignment to my colleague and I.
quests.correctedSentence: The manager gave the assignment to my colleague and me.
quests.ruleExplanation: After a preposition like 'to', the pronoun should be in the object case: 'me', not the subject form 'I'.
quests.nativeTip: This pronoun follows the preposition 'to' — should it be the subject form 'I' or the object form 'me'?

quests.faultySentence: Him and his coworkers finished the project ahead of schedule.
quests.correctedSentence: He and his coworkers finished the project ahead of schedule.
quests.ruleExplanation: Because this pronoun is the subject of the sentence, it needs the subject form 'he', not the object form 'him'.
quests.nativeTip: This pronoun is doing the action of finishing the project — subject or object form?

quests.faultySentence: The company announced it's new policy yesterday.
quests.correctedSentence: The company announced its new policy yesterday.
quests.ruleExplanation: The possessive form of 'it' has no apostrophe: 'its', while 'it's' means 'it is'. This sentence needs the possessive 'its'.
quests.nativeTip: 'It's' is a contraction for 'it is' — does this sentence need a contraction or a possessive form?

quests.faultySentence: This is mine umbrella, not yours.
quests.correctedSentence: This is my umbrella, not yours.
quests.ruleExplanation: Possessive adjectives like 'my' go before a noun, while 'mine' stands alone; since 'umbrella' follows, the sentence needs 'my umbrella'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Mine' stands alone without a noun after it — which possessive form goes directly before a noun?

quests.faultySentence: Is this laptop your's or your coworker's?
quests.correctedSentence: Is this laptop yours or your coworker's?
quests.ruleExplanation: The possessive pronoun 'yours' never takes an apostrophe, unlike a contraction, so the sentence needs 'yours', not 'your's'.
quests.nativeTip: Possessive pronouns like 'yours', 'hers', and 'ours' never take an apostrophe — does this word need one?

quests.conceptTitle: Reflexive Pronouns: Action Returns to the Subject
quests.faultySentence: She hurt her while hiking last weekend.
quests.correctedSentence: She hurt herself while hiking last weekend.
quests.ruleExplanation: When the subject and the object of the action are the same person, a reflexive pronoun is needed: 'herself', not 'her'.
quests.nativeTip: The subject and the person who got hurt are the same person — what pronoun shows that?

quests.faultySentence: He taught hisself how to play the guitar over the summer.
quests.correctedSentence: He taught himself how to play the guitar over the summer.
quests.ruleExplanation: The correct reflexive pronoun for 'he' is 'himself'; 'hisself' is a nonstandard form that isn't used in standard English.
quests.nativeTip: The standard reflexive form for 'he' is not 'hisself' — what is the correct word?

quests.conceptTitle: Reflexive Pronouns: Not Used Without a Matching Subject
quests.faultySentence: Please send the invoice to myself by Friday.
quests.correctedSentence: Please send the invoice to me by Friday.
quests.ruleExplanation: Reflexive pronouns need a matching subject in the same sentence; since there isn't one here, the simple object pronoun 'me' is correct.
quests.nativeTip: There's no 'I' earlier in the sentence for 'myself' to refer back to — what plain object pronoun fits instead?

quests.faultySentence: My sister forgot her umbrella, so I lent them mine.
quests.correctedSentence: My sister forgot her umbrella, so I lent her mine.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'my sister' is singular, the pronoun referring back to her should also be singular: 'her', not the plural 'them'.
quests.nativeTip: The antecedent is 'my sister', a single person — which pronoun matches that?

quests.faultySentence: The players celebrated because he won the championship.
quests.correctedSentence: The players celebrated because they won the championship.
quests.ruleExplanation: Because 'the players' is plural, the pronoun referring back to them must be plural: 'they', not the singular 'he'.
quests.nativeTip: 'The players' is a plural group — which pronoun matches a plural antecedent?

quests.faultySentence: My brother and his wife renovated her kitchen last year.
quests.correctedSentence: My brother and his wife renovated their kitchen last year.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the kitchen belongs to both 'my brother and his wife', the pronoun should be plural: 'their', not the singular 'her'.
quests.nativeTip: The antecedent is 'my brother and his wife' — two people together. What pronoun matches that compound subject?

quests.conceptTitle: Pronoun Agreement: Nearer Noun with Or/Nor
quests.faultySentence: Neither the teacher nor the students remembered to bring his materials.
quests.correctedSentence: Neither the teacher nor the students remembered to bring their materials.
quests.ruleExplanation: When subjects are joined by 'nor', the pronoun agrees with the nearer noun, 'the students', which is plural, so 'their' is correct.
quests.nativeTip: With 'neither...nor', the pronoun should agree with the noun closest to it — which noun is that here?

quests.conceptTitle: Pronoun Agreement: Nearer Noun with Or/Nor
quests.faultySentence: Either my parents or my sister will bring their own car.
quests.correctedSentence: Either my parents or my sister will bring her own car.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'my sister' is the noun closest to the pronoun, the singular pronoun 'her' is correct, not the plural 'their'.
quests.nativeTip: The pronoun should match whichever noun is closest to it — is that 'parents' or 'sister' here?

quests.faultySentence: Both the manager and the assistant submitted her report on time.
quests.correctedSentence: Both the manager and the assistant submitted their report on time.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Both the manager and the assistant' functions as a plural subject, so the pronoun should be plural: 'their', not the singular 'her'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Both...and' joins two subjects into a plural unit — what pronoun matches a plural subject?

quests.conceptTitle: Pronoun Case: Object Pronouns After Prepositions
quests.faultySentence: This decision is between you and I.
quests.correctedSentence: This decision is between you and me.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Between' is a preposition, and prepositions take object pronouns, so the sentence needs 'you and me', not 'you and I'.
quests.nativeTip: Prepositions like 'between' are always followed by object pronouns — is 'I' a subject or object form?

quests.conceptTitle: Pronoun Case: Object Pronouns After Prepositions
quests.faultySentence: The teacher gave extra help to him and I after class.
quests.correctedSentence: The teacher gave extra help to him and me after class.
quests.ruleExplanation: After the preposition 'to', both pronouns need the object case: 'him and me', not 'him and I'.
quests.nativeTip: This pronoun pair follows the preposition 'to' — should both be object pronouns?

quests.conceptTitle: Pronoun Case: Object Pronouns After Prepositions
quests.faultySentence: The prize was shared equally between my partner and I after the tournament.
quests.correctedSentence: The prize was shared equally between my partner and me after the tournament.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'between' is a preposition, it needs object pronouns on both sides: 'my partner and me', not 'my partner and I'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Between' takes an object pronoun — check the pronoun paired with 'my partner'.

quests.faultySentence: When the manager met with the employee, he explained the new policy.
quests.correctedSentence: When the manager met with the employee, the manager explained the new policy.
quests.ruleExplanation: Because both 'the manager' and 'the employee' could be 'he', the sentence should replace the unclear pronoun with the specific noun 'the manager', who logically would be the one explaining policy.
quests.nativeTip: The pronoun 'he' could refer to either person mentioned — which noun makes the meaning clear and logical?

quests.faultySentence: After the customer contacted the seller, they issued a refund.
quests.correctedSentence: After the customer contacted the seller, the seller issued a refund.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'they' could refer to either party, replacing it with 'the seller' removes the ambiguity, because sellers are the ones who issue refunds.
quests.nativeTip: 'They' could point to either the customer or the seller — which one logically issues a refund?

quests.faultySentence: The report was placed next to the folder before it was reviewed.
quests.correctedSentence: The report was placed next to the folder before the report was reviewed.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'it' is unclear, replacing it with 'the report' clarifies the sentence, because reports, not folders, are typically what get reviewed.
quests.nativeTip: 'It' could point to either the report or the folder — which one is more logically something that gets reviewed?

quests.faultySentence: If anyone calls, please tell him I'll call back later.
quests.correctedSentence: If anyone calls, please tell them I'll call back later.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'anyone' doesn't indicate a specific gender, the singular 'they' (here, 'them') is the appropriate pronoun, not the gendered 'him'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Anyone' doesn't specify a gender — what pronoun works for an unknown or unspecified person?

quests.faultySentence: Each employee should update her contact information by Friday.
quests.correctedSentence: Each employee should update their contact information by Friday.
quests.ruleExplanation: Because 'each employee' could refer to anyone regardless of gender, the singular 'they' ('their') is appropriate instead of assuming 'her'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Each employee' doesn't specify gender — what pronoun avoids assuming one?

quests.faultySentence: Somebody forgot his badge at the front desk; can someone check the lost and found?
quests.correctedSentence: Somebody forgot their badge at the front desk; can someone check the lost and found?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'somebody' doesn't specify gender, the sentence should use the singular 'they' ('their'), not the gendered 'his'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Somebody' doesn't tell us the person's gender — which pronoun fits an unspecified individual?

quests.conceptTitle: Pronoun Reference: Long Noun Phrases and True Antecedent
quests.faultySentence: The report about the quarterly sales figures needs revision, and they should be completed by Friday.
quests.correctedSentence: The report about the quarterly sales figures needs revision, and it should be completed by Friday.
quests.ruleExplanation: The true antecedent is 'the report', which is singular, so the pronoun should be 'it', not the plural 'they', even though 'figures' appears nearby.
quests.nativeTip: Look past 'the quarterly sales figures' — what is the true subject that needs a pronoun, 'report' or 'figures'?

quests.conceptTitle: Pronoun Reference: Long Noun Phrases and True Antecedent
quests.faultySentence: The box of old photographs from my grandmother's house needs to be sorted before we donate them.
quests.correctedSentence: The box of old photographs from my grandmother's house needs to be sorted before we donate it.
quests.ruleExplanation: The sentence is about donating 'the box', a singular noun, so the pronoun should be 'it', not the plural 'them' referring to the nearby 'photographs'.
quests.nativeTip: What are we actually planning to donate — the box itself, or is the pronoun referring to something else nearby?

quests.conceptTitle: Pronoun Reference: Long Noun Phrases and True Antecedent
quests.faultySentence: The stack of contracts waiting for approval sits on her desk, and she reviews them every afternoon.
quests.correctedSentence: The stack of contracts waiting for approval sits on her desk, and she reviews it every afternoon.
quests.ruleExplanation: The true subject is 'the stack', which is singular, so the correct pronoun is 'it', not the plural 'them' referring to 'contracts'.
quests.nativeTip: What does she review each afternoon — the stack itself, or the contracts mentioned within the phrase?

quests.faultySentence: Me and him are responsible for the budget this quarter.
quests.correctedSentence: He and I are responsible for the budget this quarter.
quests.ruleExplanation: As the subjects of the sentence, both pronouns should be in the subject case: 'he and I', not the object forms 'me and him'.
quests.nativeTip: Both pronouns are the subject performing the action — should they be subject or object forms?

quests.conceptTitle: Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement: Consistency Within a Sentence
quests.faultySentence: None of the applicants submitted their resume on the correct form, which delayed his interview.
quests.correctedSentence: None of the applicants submitted their resume on the correct form, which delayed their interview.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the antecedent was already referred to as 'their' earlier in the sentence, the second pronoun should stay consistent: 'their', not switch to 'his'.
quests.nativeTip: The sentence already used 'their' once for this antecedent — should the second pronoun match?

quests.conceptTitle: Pronoun Reference and Case: Clarity and Correct Form
quests.faultySentence: When the client emailed the consultant, them asked for an updated proposal by Friday.
quests.correctedSentence: When the client emailed the consultant, the consultant asked for an updated proposal by Friday.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Them' cannot function as a subject, and it's unclear who it refers to, so replacing it with the specific noun 'the consultant' fixes both the case and the ambiguity.
quests.nativeTip: 'Them' is an object pronoun, so it can't be the subject here, and the reference is unclear anyway — what specific noun fixes both problems?
